description: Planning to build a game/app that can simulate real life experiences and decisions that a real astronaut in training faces during his/her training
summary: SkyLab: A Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a free browser game for kids aged 7 to 12. Players lead a crew of four on a Moon or Mars outpost for 20 sols, spending limited crew hours on air, power, food and radiation shielding. Every system depends on the others, so one weak choice can cause a chain of problems. Night, dust storms, fires, air leaks and solar flares force safe decisions, and each sol ends with a real space fact and a short quiz. Sunlight and radiation levels come from real measurements, which makes Mars harder on power and the Moon harder on radiation. The game addresses the challenge by turning outpost life-support trade-offs into something students can play and learn from. It matters because understanding a space mission as a set of connected systems builds planning and problem-solving skills.
details:
What it does and how it works. The player commands a crew of four on a Moon or Mars outpost and must keep them alive for 20 sols (days). Each sol they have limited crew hours to spend on an air plant, solar panels, a greenhouse and a radiation wall. A forecast shows what will happen next sol, so players plan, test and adjust. A four-act story adds damage that carries over, so a broken system keeps hurting until the crew repairs it. Random emergencies such as fires, leaks, CO2 build-up, solar flares and dust storms teach the safe response, and each sol ends with a real space fact. A live outpost view shows the crew reacting to low oxygen, power or food. After each mission, players take a short quiz, earn XP and ranks, and can meet bonus goals.

Extra training modules deepen the learning: Mission Control (triage, timed decisions and a replay of the Apollo 13 emergency), ISS Spacewalk, Repair Mission, Moonwalk, Suit Up, Space Station Tour, Solar System Explorer and Pack the Cargo, where a weight limit forces trade-offs about what to launch.

Real data. The game uses real values for Mars and Earth sunlight (586.2 and 1361.0 W/m²), day lengths, and measured radiation on the Moon (1369 µSv/day), on Mars (624 µSv/day) and on the space station (731 µSv/day). These make Mars harder on power and the Moon harder on radiation. All other numbers are simplified game units, and the lunar day is compressed to fit 20 sols.

Benefits and intended impact. Students learn that habitats are connected systems, that every choice has a cost, and that staying calm and following a checklist saves lives. A Science and Teachers panel gives learning goals and discussion questions. The game is free, needs no account and runs offline.

Tools and technology. HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single file, the canvas for animated scenes and games, and the Web Audio API for sound effects generated in the browser. Progress is saved in the browser’s local storage. There are no external libraries and no network calls. It can be played on any devices be it smartphones, laptops or desktops.

Creativity. SkyLab turns life support into a story with consequences instead of a quiz. Damage carries over between sols, emergencies shuffle their answers so players must read carefully, and failing is treated as practice, like astronaut simulators. The game blends a survival simulation with real data, real mission events and hands-on training activities.

Factors we considered. Age-appropriate language and short text for ages 7 to 12, accuracy (simplified science, honest about what is simplified), accessibility (large buttons, keyboard and touch controls, a sound toggle, reduced-motion support), safety (no accounts or personal data) and classroom use (offline, quick sessions, and a reset button for shared devices).
